headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: xonsh can read/write broad filesystem and network, while pdf.js processes PDF files with browser-based tests, creating unsafe shared-workspace and output-trust pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A can process PDF files and run browsers, while B can read/write the filesystem and execute shell commands. If B opens or parses PDF.js outputs from a shared workspace, attacker-controlled document content could be treated as instructions. The pair lacks documented provenance tracking or isolation between their file surfaces.
conditions: IF B consumes PDF-derived text from a shared directory without sanitization
IF A's browser-based test artifacts are copied into B's shell workflow
mitigations: Separate input and output directories for the two agents
Disable automatic parsing of PDF text as commands
Add a manual review step before B consumes A's artifacts
Use read-only mounts for A's outputs
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to shared files

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches PDF documents and B reads filesystem contents with broad network egress. In a shared workspace, PDF contents can flow from A into B, and B can then transmit those contents outward. This is not proven by direct evidence, but the documented file and network surfaces make leakage plausible in default use.
conditions: IF A and B share a writable workspace
IF B is allowed to send files or logs over the network
mitigations: Keep A and B on separate workspaces
Block B network egress for sensitive runs
Restrict B to redacted inputs only
Review outbound destinations before execution
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention rules

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A supports multiple instances and works on PDF files; B can read and write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses. If both operate on the same directory, concurrent writes can corrupt artifacts or overwrite each other's outputs. Because B has no multiple-instance support and no locking is documented, the shared-write pathway is dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory
IF the orchestrator does not provide file locks
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Run only one writer at a time
Make A outputs read-only to B
Use temporary per-run subdirectories
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable paths

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate PDF-derived outputs, and B can execute shell commands and read filesystem contents. If B treats A's extracted text or test results as authoritative, errors in A can cascade into shell actions or downstream files. The pair has no documented verification gate, so the interaction is inferred and should be treated conservatively.
conditions: IF B consumes A's output without validation
IF B uses A-produced text to build shell commands or scripts
mitigations: Require human review before shell execution
Validate A outputs against a schema
Log and diff A outputs before use
Limit B to read-only analysis of A results
requires-engineering: add typed handoff contracts

E_compliance.rationale: A is a document-processing tool for PDF files, while B handles filesystem contents, source code, configuration, and environment variables. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, but they do show different data classes and retention-sensitive surfaces. Because no explicit compliance controls are documented, the gap is limited but real.
conditions: IF regulated documents are stored in the shared workspace
IF retention or deletion requirements differ between the two agents
mitigations: Classify documents before routing them
Keep regulated files out of B's workspace
Document retention expectations for both agents
Delete temporary artifacts after each run
requires-engineering: align retention and residency policies
